1.pericope_label: Leave to speak, the outstretched hand, and the address to Agrippa

schools.summary: Gill sets the leave to speak after Festus's introduction and calls the opening a handsome and artificial way of gaining the king's affection which is nevertheless no mere compliment, since Lysias, Felix and Festus were all ignorant of Jewish rites while Agrippa was master of them; Calvin explains the strategy, that Paul abandons the usual form of defence and turns his speech into doctrine, addressing the king because Festus set light by everything drawn from the law and the prophets, and derives the request for patience from the commendation itself, on the principle that the more expert a man is in Scripture the more attentive he ought to be when religion is in question.

Henry accounts for Agrippa rather than Festus granting the leave by rank, the king being the most honourable person present, bearing the title though holding only the power of other governors under the emperor, and senior to Festus without being his superior; he marks the silence that preceded the leave, since those are not the most forward to speak who are best prepared, observes that Paul needed no advocate and no Tertullus, and notes that he did not plead his appeal to Caesar as an excuse for saying nothing but embraced the opportunity of doing honour to the cause he suffered for.

Barnes takes the gesture for the usual posture of public speakers, described from the ancient statues and the clasp of the outer robe, and lists three aims of the defence, none of them release: to vindicate Paul's character before Agrippa, to put the case correctly before the emperor as Festus desired, and to preach to the whole company. Ellicott adds the chain to the picture and finds a union of frankness and courtesy in an address that praises Agrippa's knowledge without praising his character. Robertson presses the wording of the leave as making Agrippa master of ceremonies over Festus, reads the verb as an inchoative imperfect, judges this the fullest of Paul's defences and free of all resentment, glosses expert as connoisseur, notes Agrippa's charge of the temple and the high priesthood, and reports the accusative that follows as an anacoluthon or an accusative absolute.

Clarke denies that the gesture was a rhetorical flourish, taking it merely as a bid for attention, and reconstructs the attitude down to the clenched third and fourth fingers. Wesley puts the chain into the same picture, calling the outstretched hand a decent expression of Paul's earnestness, divides customs and questions into the practical and the speculative, notes that questions was Festus's own word here repeated and explained, and closes with an appraisal of the whole discourse as uniting the seriousness of the Christian, the boldness of the apostle and the politeness of the gentleman and the scholar.

debates: Whether the opening is flattery: Gill calls it artificial though sincere, Barnes says Paul could not flatter but would commend as far as truth allowed, Ellicott that he praises the knowledge and not the man, and Robertson reports Blass comparing the opening to Tertullus while insisting Paul says only what is true
How the accusative in the third verse is to be construed: Knowling as an anacoluthon, Buttmann as an accusative absolute, Page as governed by the sense of thinking or considering
outliers: Robertson lists what made Agrippa competent: he had the care of the temple, the appointment of the high priest, and the keeping of the sacred vestments

Henry observes that Paul, though an apostle, never imagined that his office exempted him from the jurisdiction of the civil powers, magistracy being an ordinance all benefit by and all must be subject to
Wesley notes that the adverb rendered patiently occurs nowhere else in the New Testament

4.pericope_label: The life known from youth, the strictest sect, and the hope of the promise

schools.summary: Gill takes the closing question to be aimed at heathens and Sadducees, whether the governor and the chief captains or Agrippa himself, whom he suspects of Sadducean leanings. Calvin explains why the narrative begins so far back, that Paul must clear away the clouds of evil opinion before he can be heard with purged ears, reads the superlative strictest against the grain as praising the Pharisees' learning rather than their holiness while the Sadducees stuck to the bare letter and the Essenes cared little for doctrine, presses the covenant itself as profiting Israel nothing without the promised Mediator, warns that Luke preserves only a brief sum of a longer argument, and closes on the power of God against men who will not let his arm reach further than their own reason.

Barnes supplies the history of Paul's schooling under Gamaliel and the commission against the Christians that proves he was known, joins the Messiah and the resurrection as two halves of one hope argued each from the other, and notes that the closing pronoun is plural and that only an outline of the argument survives. Ellicott restricts all the Jews to those of Judaea, prefers most rigid to the English double superlative, renders the noun as our twelve-tribed nation while tracing the legend of the lost ten tribes to the apocryphal Esdras, and suspects Agrippa of alliance with the Sadducean high priests he had himself nominated. Robertson marks the particles that carry Paul from exordium to narrative, notes that the word for manner of life is otherwise unknown in the New Testament, calls strictest one of only three true superlatives of its form, and reports Page's view that these verses are a parenthesis showing Paul's life in Christ to be a development of the best in Pharisaism.

Clarke names the three sects and their reputations, guesses that Paul was sent up to Jerusalem at about twelve when male children were first brought to the yearly feasts, argues firmly that the hope of the promise is the resurrection and not the Messiah since the tribes are said to hope to attain to it in the very verb Paul uses of the resurrection in Philippians, and adds that two attributes stand pledged to the raising, God's truth for the promise and his power for the performance. Wesley catches the sting in the condition, that they would not testify because they knew what weight Paul's former life would add to his present witness, and holds that a great part of the ten tribes had at various times returned from the east.

debates: What the hope of the promise is: Clarke insists on the resurrection alone and excludes the Messiah on the grounds that the tribes hope to attain to it, Ellicott takes it for the whole expectation of a divine kingdom with Christ at its head, Barnes and Robertson join the two as inseparable
Why the Pharisees were called the strictest sect: Clarke for strictness of doctrine and moral practice, Calvin expressly not for holiness of life but for sincerity of doctrine and greater learning
Whether Agrippa himself doubted the resurrection: Barnes finds no evidence he did and refers the plural to Festus and his company, while Gill and Ellicott both suspect him of Sadducean leanings
outliers: Calvin turns the appeal to the consent of the Church against the Papists, arguing that Paul names the twelve tribes to mean only those who retained the true study of godliness, not all who came of Jacob according to the flesh
Robertson calls the appeal to the Jews own hope a neat turning of the tables, since Paul is accused by the very people whose mainspring that hope was
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1, 12 and 24 only, so this entry carries no comment of his and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from its tags

9.pericope_label: The persecutor: conscience, the vote against the saints, and the madness of zeal

schools.summary: Gill hears the verse as a correction of the question just asked, since Paul had no right to wonder at an unbelief that had once been his own settled judgment, and sets the particulars in Jerusalem where he consented to Stephen's death. Calvin argues from the abruptness that Luke has abridged the speech, holds that the conversion is rehearsed to prove a commandment from heaven rather than merely to clear Paul of levity, refuses to soften the compelling to blaspheme and infers real corruption among the first fruits of believers, and makes the confession itself the point, that Paul willingly utters his shame so the mercy of God may appear the more, against men who are ashamed to own an offence of ignorance and who paint or lessen what they ought to weep over.

Barnes makes the conscientiousness the hinge of the defence, since a man may be conscientious in enormous wickedness and only a demonstration as strong as conscience could have turned him, denies that Paul sat in the Sanhedrin and renders the vote as joining with those who condemned, and seizes on the madness of persecuting men for their opinions. Ellicott catches a tone of sympathy and hope toward Agrippa, finds courage in the very word saints, judges it more probable that others died beside Stephen, holds that Paul must have belonged to the Sanhedrin or a delegated tribunal, and reads the imperfect as leaving open whether any believer yielded. Robertson notes the literary construction, glosses the imprisoning verb as shutting a trapdoor, takes the vote literally as a black pebble with the consequence that Paul was then married and later a widower, and draws the hunting metaphor out of the verb for persecuting.

Clarke reads the verse as implying martyrdoms besides Stephen's whose names are not given, insists that only a madman persecutes another for differing in religious opinion and that the fiercest persecutor is the most furious madman, and places the strange cities outside Jewish jurisdiction. Wesley dates the thought to the years when Paul was a Pharisee, suggests that the chief priests may have given him a vote for the occasion, and turns the compelling to blaspheme into a direct address to the enemies of the gospel, warning them by the case of Spira, who was compelled and suffered terribly, of what awaits those who compel like Saul but do not repent like him.

debates: Whether Paul sat on the Sanhedrin: Robertson takes the black pebble literally and infers that he was then married, Ellicott that he belonged to that court or a delegated tribunal, Barnes denies it and reads the phrase as approval only, Wesley suggests a vote granted for the occasion

Whether Christians died besides Stephen: Barnes notes the silence of the history but allows it, Clarke and Ellicott both think it probable, Ellicott adding that the words about not yet resisting unto blood must then belong elsewhere
Whether the compelling succeeded: Ellicott and Robertson find room in the imperfect tense to hope that no believer yielded, Calvin takes the participle to mean that many did
outliers: Calvin infers from the compelling to blaspheme that there was great corruption even among the first fruits of believers, who under fear or stripes not only denied their Lord but spoke evil of his name
Robertson notes that Paul names the chief priests, who were Sadducees, though himself a Pharisee, both parties co-operating against the saints
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1, 12 and 24 only, so this entry carries no comment of his and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from its tags

12.pericope_label: The errand to Damascus, the light above the sun, and the voice in the Hebrew tongue

schools.summary: Gill places the errand at Damascus where believers had settled after fleeing Jerusalem, observes that the hour is a circumstance the earlier accounts omit and that Paul names the king to fix his attention, and records the difficulty that all here fall to the earth while the earlier account leaves the company standing speechless. Calvin reads the whole narration as an argument that this was no empty apparition nor a trance that robbed the man of judgment, since one who fell for fear yet heard a plain voice, asked who spoke and understood the answer was plainly not beside himself, and so did not rashly change his mind but obeyed a heavenly oracle rather than go on striving against God.

Henry presses how little the change owed to anything in Paul, whose persecuting fury was neither spent nor tired and who held as ample a commission as ever when a superior power obliged him to surrender it for another; he turns the circumstances of the light into an argument against delusion, since it came at midday in the open road and shone round the companions who all fell with him, and contrasts the thick darkness God made his pavilion in Old Testament times with the great light in which Christ now appears. He reads the goad as caution rather than threat, and dwells on the naming and on Christ claiming his followers' sufferings as his own, so that Paul, trampling on those he counted the blemishes of the earth, was insulting the glory of heaven.

Ellicott divides the warrant into the general power delegated and the specific work for which Paul was answerable, and confirms that the reading of the proverb is beyond doubt here whatever be thought of it elsewhere. Robertson notes that the word for commission occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, that the comparison with the sun stands alone among the three accounts and marks the light as supernatural, that Luke makes no attempt to harmonise the three, that the proverb is genuine here though absent from the earlier accounts and is found in Aeschylus, and that Blass sees a mark of Paul's culture in his use of a Greek and Latin proverb before this audience. Barnes, on a narrative already told twice, refers the reader back to the ninth chapter without further comment.

Clarke likewise refers the whole account back to his notes on the ninth chapter rather than expounding it again. Wesley observes that Paul turns to the king most seasonably at the height of the narration, that the light's outshining the sun is no marvel since the created sun is nothing to the Sun of righteousness, and that Paul was not then speaking Hebrew and did not trouble to say so when he was, concluding that Christ used the tongue both on earth and from heaven.

Cyril of Jerusalem takes the passage past the narrative into the dispensation behind it, wondering that the Spirit confined the other apostles to a few epistles but granted the former persecutor fourteen, not because Peter or John was less but that the doctrine might be beyond question coming from the very enemy; and he has Paul answer the general amazement at his change by owning that he did it in ignorance, thinking the preaching of Christ was the destruction of the Law and not knowing that he came to fulfil it.

debates: Whether the three accounts of the conversion can be harmonised in detail: Gill raises the difficulty that all fall here while the earlier account leaves the company standing, and Robertson answers that Luke makes no attempt to harmonise the phrasing and that Paul blends the direct words of Christ with the later message through Ananias
Whether the goad is threat or caution: Henry takes it as a warning designed to affect Paul rather than affront him, Robertson as a proverb of an ox that kicks and takes a severer wound
outliers: Robertson follows Blass in reading Paul's use of a Greek and Latin proverb, omitted in the earlier telling, as chosen for the culture of this particular audience

Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all decline to expound this narrative a third time and simply refer the reader to the ninth chapter, so that the apparent breadth of witness at these verses is thinner than the list of names suggests
themes: persecution of Christ in his members

16.pericope_label: Rise and stand: the commission to open eyes and turn men from the power of Satan

schools.summary: Gill reads the command to rise as a bidding to take heart, the appearance being for honour and not destruction, and takes the opening of the eyes as the enlightening of the understanding, wholly the Spirit's work and ascribed to the apostle only as instrument. Calvin holds that Christ threw Paul down to humble him and raises him gently, coming not as an avenger for the stripes and bloody sentences but as a merciful Lord meaning to use the man's industry; he observes what is not promised, since Paul is armed against fear but never told that those he benefits will receive him gladly, the world using the ministers of salvation as frantic men rail upon their physicians; and he defends the transfer to ministers of honour due to God alone as commending the Spirit's working rather than lessening it, reads the verse as a key to open the gate of heaven, and rejects the narrower construction of the closing words.

Barnes thinks many circumstances of the conversion went unrecorded and that Paul dwells on these because they carry his authority for preaching to the Gentiles, and draws from the title of witness the rule that a preacher must testify to what he has felt and not only to what he can prove. Ellicott takes the fuller report to embody the substance of the visions of those days of blindness, notes that a man in contact with the supernatural does not record the sequence of his thoughts like a shorthand writer, sets this passage against the account that dates the Gentile mission from the trance in the Temple and sides with Galatians, finds in the verb for sending the warrant of Paul's apostleship, and raises the construction of the closing words. Robertson hears an emphatic assonance in the two imperatives, notes that the reading makes Paul a personal eyewitness of the risen Christ, reports Page's rendering of the passive future as the visions in which Christ would be seen, and records the genuine ambiguity of the participle that may mean either delivering or choosing.

Clarke presses the first title as an under-rower who acts wholly under another's authority, so that Paul must tug at the oar to bring the vessel through a tempestuous ocean to harbour, and the second as martyr in the later sense, ancient history reporting that Paul was beheaded at Rome by Nero's command; he argues from the word for forgiveness, which signifies the removal of sins, that purification and not pardon only is meant, confirmed by the inheritance being among the sanctified, and that salvation is received by faith and so by no merit of works or sufferings. Wesley marks the pronoun as the authority of the sender and the adverb as the date of the mission, since Paul's apostleship began with his conversion, and observes that he opens their eyes who sends Paul, and does it by the Paul he sends.

debates: Whether the participle in the seventeenth verse means delivering or choosing: Robertson reports that the old Greek and the papyri support both, that either makes good sense, and that modern scholars are divided

When the mission to the Gentiles was given: Ellicott notes that the earlier account connects it with the trance in the Temple three years after the conversion, while this passage and Galatians date it from the conversion itself

How the closing words are to be construed: Ellicott allows them with either sanctified or receive and prefers the latter on internal grounds, Robertson takes them with the participle, Calvin insists the clause governs the whole period
outliers: Calvin traces the Jews' hatred of Paul not to zeal for the covenant, which he calls their pretence, but to ambition, since they alone would be excellent and all others underlings
Clarke reports from ancient history that Paul was beheaded at Rome by the command of Nero, making the title of witness a title of martyrdom in the later sense
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1, 12 and 24 only, so this entry carries no comment of his and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from its tags

19.pericope_label: Not disobedient to the heavenly vision: the preaching, the seizure, and its substance

schools.summary: Gill follows the itinerary from Damascus and sets the sufferings of Christ in the human nature, referring them to the types and the sacrifices. Calvin states the purpose of the whole rehearsal, that God was the author of everything the Jews condemned as sacrilege, refuses to let conversion and repentance be parted and charges those who separate the grace of Christ from repentance with perverting the gospel, turns the seizure against the accusers on the ground that men with a good cause would have gone to law where they had every advantage, holds that God reaches out his hand only where he acknowledges his minister and that we are not spared in order to live idly, makes the primacy in rising a matter of cause rather than of time, and gathers under the word light all that belongs to perfect felicity, hearing in it the prophecies of Isaiah.

Barnes reads the litotes simply, that the proof being clear Paul thought it his duty to begin at once, traces the deliverance past Lysias to God as those with just views always will, and denies that the primacy in rising can be first in time since Elijah and Christ himself had raised the dead, making it first in eminence. Ellicott renders the verb strictly as I did not become disobedient and finds it significant for grace and freedom, notes that the summary verb stands after the list of hearers and that Cilicia is implied before Antioch, divides the message into repentance, turning and works, names the teaching of the Gentiles as the one cause of the hostility, observes that the noun for help occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and describes an ally's aid to a weaker friend, defends the received reading of small and great, and ends on the order of the names, Moses being added as an afterthought for hearers who put the Pentateuch above the Prophets. Robertson notes that the adverb gathers up all that precedes, explains the difficult accusative as one of extent, calls the perfect I stand a picture of Paul's stability, and insists the verbal means that the Christ can suffer rather than must.

Clarke reckons some three years at Damascus and in Arabia before the journey to Jerusalem, reduces the causes of the seizure to four and notes that the charges of defiling the temple and of disloyalty are not mentioned because the adversaries had dropped them, reports the expedient of two Messiahs, one of David to reign and one of Ephraim to suffer, as having not the smallest foundation in the whole Bible, and makes the primacy in rising a rising to die no more, giving in Christ's own person the proof of the resurrection of the body. Wesley presses the litotes into doctrine, that having received power to obey Paul used it, so that even the grace which moved him was not irresistible, and puts the order shortly, that this repentance is previous both to inward and outward holiness.

debates: Whether the litotes leaves room for resistance: Ellicott finds in it the possibility of disobedience even in the vessel of election and an act of will in the passage from rebellion to obedience, and Wesley concludes outright that the grace which moved Paul was not irresistible

In what sense Christ is the first to rise: Barnes takes it for eminence and not order, since others had been raised before, Clarke for the first who rose to die no more, Calvin for cause rather than time, Christ in rising becoming conqueror of death
Whether the Christ must suffer or can: Robertson and Ellicott both read the verbal as capability rather than necessity, a form found here alone in the New Testament
outliers: Clarke argues that since Paul preached nothing but what Moses and the prophets had said, they must have spoken of the resurrection of the dead, which he takes to refute the view that the immortality of the soul was unknown to the ancient Jews
Ellicott rejects the variant that would make Paul witnessed to by small and great, on the ground that it was never true that he had a good report of all men
Robertson observes that in this speech it is the word resurrection, and not the word Gentiles as in the speech from the stairs, that provokes the interruption
Matthew Henry keys his notes to verses 1, 12 and 24 only, so this entry carries no comment of his and the puritan-evangelical school is absent from its tags

24.pericope_label: Festus interrupts: much learning, the words of truth and soberness, and the appeal to Agrippa

schools.summary: Gill notes that the title of honour is given by custom and not by fear or flattery, and grounds the appeal in Agrippa's acquaintance with the prophetic writings and with the report of their fulfilment. Calvin makes the outcry a case of the truth being trodden under foot by pride, Festus granting recondite learning in the speech yet counting the man frenzied because the gospel is hidden from unbelievers, and refusing to attend lest he be made mad himself as many still fly from the word lest they drown in a labyrinth; he observes that Paul does not vaunt his wit or defend his wisdom but is content with the single plea that he teaches nothing but what is true and sober, and sees the turn to Agrippa as deliberate, the king being granted the history only to be called back to the law and the prophets, and his faith assumed less to praise him than to put the Scripture beyond question.

Henry weighs the manner of the interruption, spoken aloud rather than whispered and without consulting the king to whom Festus had lately professed deference, so that Paul should be obliged to break off and the hearers diverted, and judges it spoken not so much in anger as in scorn; he finds the reproach double-edged, the fishermen apostles being despised for having no learning and Paul, bred a Pharisee, for having too much, and recalls that the old prophets were stigmatised the same way. He draws from Paul's courtesy the lesson that we are not to render railing for railing but to speak civilly of those who speak slightly of us, and holds that all the country rang of these things, so that it was a shame to Festus to be ignorant of what Agrippa could not but know.

Barnes lists what would have provoked the charge, Paul's earnestness, the weight laid on a despised Nazarene and the story of the vision taken for delirium, observes how commonly the charge is still made against unusual zeal, admires the turn by which Paul appeals at once to Agrippa and makes him the witness, and holds it evidence of honesty when a man will declare everything without reserve before those qualified to detect him. Ellicott takes the neuter plural strictly as thy many writings, the word being one the Jews used of their sacred books which Festus knew Paul was always studying, notes the union of calm protest with courtesy and the ethical weight of the word for soberness, and makes the appeal twofold, to the prophets and to the communities that had rested for a quarter of a century on the belief that the Christ had come and risen. Robertson marks the genitive absolute, the predicative adjective and the linear present of the verb, and notes that both the verb for speaking forth and the verb for the king's knowing belong to the literary language rather than the vernacular.

Clarke thinks Festus meant no more than that a vast variety of knowledge had overcharged the brain, since Paul makes no show of learning here and quotes none of the celebrated authors as he had at Athens but spoke of spiritual things a Roman heathen could not conceive; he calls the reply the fullest proof of sound sense that could have been given, finds the two Greek words elegantly opposed, and notes that an apostle may address men in power in terms that taken literally imply more than they deserve. Wesley turns the charge back on the governor, who saw that nature did not act in Paul but did not see the grace that did, exclaims at the reply that mad men seldom call men by their names and titles of honour, and suspects that the very freedom of Paul's speech was one thing Festus took for madness.

debates: What the much learning was: Ellicott takes the neuter plural for the sacred writings Festus knew Paul studied, Clarke for a general excess of knowledge overcharging the brain, Henry for the study that let Paul cite books the governor was a stranger to

In what spirit Festus spoke: Henry judges it scorn rather than anger and notes the candid construction he put on the supposed delirium, Barnes takes it for genuine amazement at Paul's zeal, Ellicott hears a loud laugh of scorn from a governor who had forgotten the dignity of his office
outliers: Ellicott reads the notice of the loud voice as one of the touches of vividness that show the writer relating what he had actually heard

Calvin holds that Agrippa, though he did not reverence Scripture as a godly man should, had from childhood the persuasion that it contains nothing but the oracles of God, which is why Paul can rest his case on it
Robertson notes the unusual position of the pronoun between the adjective and the noun in the charge of much learning

27.pericope_label: Believest thou the prophets? Agrippa’s answer and the wish for all that heard him

schools.summary: Gill takes the question of what the prophets said concerning the person, sufferings and resurrection of Christ and whether these were fulfilled in Jesus, allows that Agrippa's answer might be serious or ironical and inclines to the former, and marks Paul's reply as a prayer showing both his affection for souls and his sense that grace is necessary. Calvin reports the divided history of the phrase, Valla rendering it almost and the older interpreter leaving it word for word, suggests that it may fitly be referred to time as though Agrippa said Paul would make him a Christian in a moment, grants that the sense almost is not to be disliked, and reads the confession as wrung out of a man who could no longer resist the truth and was drawn against his will, which shows how great the pride of nature is until the Spirit brings it under.

Barnes calls the address an instance of Paul's happy manner, brought in to meet the charge of derangement with the king's own testimony, treats the answer as a candid avowal and the moment as the crisis of Agrippa's life, since to be almost persuaded and go no further is the very position of guilt and danger, and reads the reply as a petition showing that Paul knew nothing but grace would overcome the reluctance of the human heart. Ellicott notes that a Jew could not before other Jews speak of the Law and the Prophets as Festus had spoken of Paul's learning, denies that the Greek will bear the familiar rendering and takes the answer for a cynical sneer, evasive as well as derisive, citing the older English versions against Geneva, lays out three possible constructions of Paul's reply and prefers the one that keeps both conjunctions in their natural force, and hears an almost plaintive pathos in the closing words. Robertson puts the question as a trap sprung, since yes would place Agrippa in Paul's hands and no would deny the prophets, judges the tone of the answer ironical but not unpleasant, and notes the courteous optative of the reply.

Clarke sets out the inference the king was meant to draw, reads his words as the genuine effusion of a heart persuaded of the truth and kept from confessing it only by secular considerations, and says he cannot understand how anyone weighing the circumstances could take them for irony; he has the apostle lifting the chain, probably now detached from the soldier and wrapped about his own arm, and observes that the council could bear the scene no longer but rose at once and echoed his very word in their verdict. Wesley says Paul now comes close to the heart, sets Festus altogether a heathen and Paul altogether a Christian with Agrippa halting between the two, and notes that Agrippa had spoken of being a Christian as a thing wholly in his own power, which Paul gently corrects by making it the gift and work of God.

Cyril of Jerusalem, treating these hearings together as one witness to the Spirit's power, ascribes the whole to grace: when Paul was set amid the tribunals of justice, before Felix at one time and before Festus the governor and King Agrippa at another, he obtained of the Holy Ghost a grace so great and so triumphant in wisdom.

debates: What Agrippa’s answer means: Clarke takes it for sincere conviction and rejects irony outright, Barnes for a candid avowal and the crisis of his life, Gill allows either and inclines to the serious reading, Ellicott makes it a cynical and evasive sneer, Robertson an ironical but not unpleasant shrug, and Calvin a confession wrung out against the will

Whether the Greek can mean almost: Ellicott and Robertson both deny it and render in or with a little, Calvin reports Valla for almost and does not dislike the sense, and the English versions divide, Wyclif, Tyndale and the Rhemish against Geneva
How Paul’s answering phrase is to be construed: Ellicott gives three possible paraphrases and prefers the one keeping both conjunctions copulative, Robertson renders it both in little and in great
outliers: Clarke observes that the council’s verdict echoes Paul’s own last word, bonds, which he takes as evidence of the impression the lifted chain had made

Calvin notes that Paul wishes the others his own faith but not his own trouble, since men who did not yet believe were far from being ready to strive for the gospel, and calls it a courtesy far contrary to the bitterness of those who take comfort in wishing others in their misery

30.pericope_label: The court rises: the unanimous verdict and the appeal that could not be undone

schools.summary: Gill records that the opening clause is missing from the Alexandrian copy and from the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic versions, that the company withdrew into an apartment adjoining the judgment hall, and that Agrippa gives his opinion by way of advice only, the determination lying with the governor. Calvin turns the verdict on Festus, who in agreeing with the rest condemns himself, having brought Paul into these straits by unjust dealing and endangered his life under colour of changing the place; and he holds that the appeal, though it seems to have hindered the apostle, was the only way of escaping death, so that Paul is content with it both because matters were no longer entire and because the vision had told him he was called to Rome.

Robertson notes that the verb of rising agrees with the king alone and that the entertainment was over, describes the conference as the eager talk of dignitaries about a wonderful speech, presses the awkwardness of a verdict unanimous among Romans, Jews and Greeks which leaves Festus to explain why the man was not long since free, adds that Paul had won none of them to Christ, and reads the closing sentence as a condition contrary to fact. Barnes counts the concurring witnesses, Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, and takes the king's remark for a full declaration of his conviction and an instance of bold dealing ending well. Ellicott reads the rising as a sign that the words had told and notes that Paul was afterwards treated with more respect, explains why the historian dwells on the acquittal, since the charge of revolutionary tendencies was too current against the apostle and his followers to be passed over, and finds in the decision a vindication of Paul's course, the matter now being neither hushed up nor disposed of by a release that would have exposed him to conspiracy.

Wesley calls the rising an unspeakably precious moment for Agrippa and leaves it there, whether he improved it or not being a thing to be seen in that day, and refuses to let the verdict pass as a compliment, noting that they speak of the whole life and not of one action, and asking whether nothing more could be learned from such a discourse, since a favourable judgment of such a preacher is not all that God requires. Clarke says the king was prompted to wish an immediate release which the registered appeal had made impracticable, and reports Bishop Pearce's conjecture that Agrippa afterwards represented the case so favourably at Rome that Paul was soon at liberty there, which would also explain the courtesy shown him by the centurion on the voyage.

Chrysostom presses the providence in the outcome: they acquit as undeserving even of bonds the man they had just called mad, and would have released him outright but for the appeal; yet it was ordered so that he should go bound, for if his Lord was reckoned among the transgressors much more might he be, and the marvel is that one so mixed up with such men should take no harm from them.

debates: Why Paul was not released: Robertson holds that he certainly could have been and that Festus comes out with no honour, Clarke that the registered appeal had made it impracticable, Calvin and Chrysostom both that the appeal was providential, the one because it was the only escape from death, the other because Paul was meant to go to Rome in bonds
outliers: Clarke reports Bishop Pearce's conjecture that Agrippa spoke for Paul at Rome, and traces to it both the courtesy of the centurion on the voyage and the liberty of the two years in a hired house

Ellicott follows Agrippa's later career out of Josephus, the banqueting hall overlooking the Temple courts, the wall the Jews built to block his view, the embassy that won Poppaea's support against Festus, and the completion of the Temple ten years before he saw it destroyed
Robertson notes that for all the unanimity of the verdict Paul had won none of these dignitaries to Christ
